title: Screening vs Buffing vs Sanding Hardwood Floors: What Each One Actually Does
meta: Buffing polishes, screening scuffs the old finish for a new coat, and sanding goes to bare wood. Wills Flooring explains which one your Lynnwood floor needs.
keywords: screening vs sanding hardwood floors, buff and coat hardwood floors, screen and recoat vs refinish, what is screening a hardwood floor, hardwood floor buffing cost, Lynnwood hardwood floor refinishing

blocks.lead: Buffing polishes the finish you have, screening scuffs that finish so a new coat will stick, and sanding removes the finish and a thin layer of wood so the floor starts over.
blocks.detail: Only screening and sanding are refinishing services. At Wills Flooring a screen and recoat is $1.99 per sq ft, a full sand and natural finish is $3.99, and sand with stain is $6.50, all with a 500 sq ft minimum.

blocks.html: The three words get used interchangeably online, and that is how a Lynnwood homeowner ends up paying for a full sanding when a recoat would have done, or paying for a "buff and coat" that peels a year later because the floor should have been sanded. Alderwood and Martha Lake are full of 1960s to 1980s ramblers and split-levels with red oak strip floors, and every one of them sits in a different place on this ladder. Here is what each refinishing process actually does to the wood.

blocks.text: Buffing: what it is and what it is not

blocks.html: Buffing is a cleaning and polishing step. A rotary buffer with a soft pad works a cleaner or polish across the floor and brings back some shine on a floor that is dull from dirt rather than wear. It does not remove finish and it does not add durable finish. It suits a floor that looks tired but has no scratches, and most homeowners can do it with a rental buffer. Any quote that offers to "buff and coat" your floor is really describing a screen and recoat. Ask which abrasive they are using.

blocks.title: The polish trap:
blocks.text: Off-the-shelf floor polishes and acrylic restorers leave a plastic film that new finish will not stick to. If a floor has been polished for years, it usually cannot be screened; the film has to be chemically stripped or the floor sanded. Tell us what has been used on the floor before we quote a recoat.

items.title: How it works
items.text: A mesh abrasive screen under a buffer, or fine paper on a multi-disc sander, dulls and lightly cuts the existing finish so a fresh coat has something to grip. The old finish stays; you are adding a wear layer on top of it. One coat of Bona water-based finish goes on the same day.

items.title: When it is the right answer
items.text: The finish is intact everywhere, the wear is surface scratches and dull traffic lanes, and you like the color. A screen every five to seven years on a Lynnwood family floor can put off a full sanding for decades, and the wood never gets thinner.

items.title: When it fails
items.text: Any spot where the finish has worn through to bare wood, gray boards near a slider, pet stains, or a floor that was waxed or polished. New finish over bare or contaminated wood looks blotchy and peels. We check with a water drop test at the estimate.

items.title: The math on a typical Lynnwood main floor
items.text: A 750 sq ft rambler main floor in Meadowdale is 750 × $1.99 = $1,493 for a screen and recoat, against 750 × $3.99 = $2,993 for a full sanding. Same day in and out, half the price. That gap is why we always ask the recoat question first.

blocks.text: Price your Lynnwood floor right now

blocks.note: Choose Recoat if your finish is intact everywhere. Choose Natural or Stain if the floor has bare spots, deep scratches or a color you want to change.

blocks.text: Sanding: when the floor has to start over

items.text: A belt sander with coarse paper takes off the finish and the top of the wood. This is where scratches, gray, old stain and most pet marks disappear. Edges and closets are done with an edger.
items.note: About 1/32 in of wood per full sanding. A 3/4 in solid floor can take this several times over its life.

items.text: Two more passes with finer paper remove the scratch pattern from the previous grit. Filler goes into gaps and nail holes between passes. A multi-disc sander blends the field and the edges so no swirl marks show under the finish.

items.d: Day 2 · Stain, if you chose it
items.text: The floor is water-popped to open the grain, stained by hand and left to dry overnight. This is the step that turns 1970s orange oak into a light or dark modern floor, and it is the reason stain costs more.
Bona water-based finish, three coats, with a light abrasion between coats. You can walk in socks the morning after the last coat and move furniture back after about three days.

blocks.text: Which one does your floor need?

items.html: Do the water test. A drop of water in the busiest spot and in front of the slider. Beads up: the finish is intact and screening is possible. Soaks in and darkens: that spot is bare and the floor needs sanding.
Check the sunny spots. Gray or bleached boards in front of south windows in a Martha Lake living room mean the finish failed there years ago. Sanding only.
Decide about color. If you want the floor lighter, darker or less orange, that is sanding plus stain. No amount of screening changes color.
Tell us the history. Wax, polish, oil soap and DIY recoats all change the answer. We would rather know before we quote than find out when the first coat fisheyes.

blocks.text: Mistakes that cost Lynnwood homeowners money

items: Paying for a full sanding on a five-year-old floor with surface scratches. That is a $1.99 job billed at $3.99.
Accepting a "buff and coat" on a floor with bare spots. The new coat peels along the traffic lane within a year and the floor gets sanded anyway.
Screening over a polished floor. It looks fine on day one and fails when the film under it lets go.
Sanding a thin floor that has already been done three or four times. We check the thickness at a heat register before we cut.

faq.q: What is the difference between screening and sanding a hardwood floor?
faq.a: Screening abrades only the top of the existing finish so one new coat can bond; the wood is never exposed. Sanding removes all the finish and about 1/32 in of wood, then rebuilds the floor with three coats. Screening costs $1.99 per sq ft at Wills Flooring, sanding $3.99 natural or $6.50 with stain.

faq.q: Is buffing the same as a screen and recoat?
faq.a: No. Buffing uses a soft pad to clean or polish the existing finish and adds nothing durable. A screen and recoat uses an abrasive screen to scuff the finish and then applies a new coat of finish. When a contractor says buff and coat, they almost always mean a screen and recoat; ask which abrasive they use.

faq.q: How do I know if my floor can be screened instead of sanded?
faq.a: Put a drop of water on the worst traffic spot. If it beads, the finish is intact there and screening will work. If it soaks in and darkens the wood, that area is bare and needs sanding. Floors that have been waxed or polished usually cannot be screened either, because new finish will not bond to the film.

faq.q: How often should hardwood floors be screened and recoated?
faq.a: Every five to seven years in a normal Lynnwood household, sooner with big dogs or a busy entry. The point is to add finish before the old finish wears through. Once you can see bare wood, the recoat window has closed and the next step is a full sanding at roughly twice the price.

faq.q: Can screening change the color or sheen of my floor?
faq.a: It can change the sheen: you can go from a semi-gloss to satin or matte with the new coat. It cannot change the color, because the stain sits under the old finish that stays in place. Any color change, including removing the orange tone of older red oak, requires sanding to bare wood and staining.
